latin.298:
ANNOTATIO VI.
De Controversiarum, quae Evangelicis intercedunt, Classibus ad p.353.356.
J. 1.
Citè admodum Autor noster in DUAS majores controversias dirimit, attendendo discrimen fere triplex, quô Classes istae duae inter se discriminantur, scilicet Autorum, Numeri, & Modi Controversias tractandi.
latin.299: Prior Classis juxta Autorem nostrum, Disputatores habet genuinos Lutheri, (puta placidioris, fidissimi charissimique Symmystae sui Philippi Melanchtonis variatam i. e. declaratam explicatamque August. Confessionem, etiam quod ad Xmum Articul. de Coena Sacra attinet,) si non à priori, à posteriori tamen, admittentis & approbantis, discipulos, vid. Annot. I. §.6.
latin.300: Numerum, fere ad Unitatem redactum, non de reali corporis & sanguinis Christi in coena Praesentia & Manducatione supernaturalibus & spiritualibus utrinque concessis, sed de Praesentia, in, cum, & sub pane contingente, manducationeque orali, tàm indignorum quàm dignorum Communicantium.
latin.301: Modum tractandi placidum & qualis decet, Controversiam Theologicam ab utraque contendentium parte habitam minus fundamentalem, ut scilicet charitati fraternae Christianaeque locus maneat reliquus.
latin.302: Haec controversiarum Theologicarum Classis, ad quemcunque tandem numerum extensâ, Lutheranos inter & Reformatos, quà rem, non alia est, quàm qualis inter ipsos vel Lutheranos, e. g. de Omnipraesentia & Multipraesentia Corporis Christi; Vel Reformatos, e. g. de Universali & Particulari Gratia, adhuc dum viget, Unioni Ecclesiasticae nihil quicquam derogans.
latin.303: Unde dubium non est, quòd sicuti Reformatis agnita quondam Lutheranorum horum secum inita Fraternitas, tùm in Germania inter Marpurgenses & Rintelenses, Cassellis, tùm in Polonia inter Augustana, Bohemica & Helvetica Confessionis, Sendomiriae est; Reformati etiam hodieque, ut semper aliàs, cum hujusmodi Lutheranis Fraternitatem Christianam sibi intercedere apertè profitentur; Ita non minus Lutheranos hos, corda animosque suos, cum Reformatis fraterno amore, etsi occultius conjunxisse, ab externa licèt Fraternitatis professione, metu Schismatis, quô reliqui Lutherani à se scinderentur, cohibiti.
latin.304: Quod enim nullo omnino fundamentali errore Reformati à se diffideant, pridem tenent, non minus, ac Reformati Lutheranos hosce ab omni prorsus errore fundamentali immunes dudum agnoverunt & celebrarunt.

pass_a.298: ANNOTATION VI. On the Classes of Controversies that stand between Evangelicals, at pp. 353–356. J. 1. Quite quickly our Author divides them into TWO major controversies, attending to an almost triple distinction by which those two Classes are discriminated from each other — namely of Authors, of Number, and of the Mode of treating Controversies.
pass_a.299: The Prior Class, according to our Author, has as Disputators the genuine disciples of Luther — those who admit and approve (if not a priori, yet a posteriori) the Augsburg Confession as varied, that is declared and explained, by his milder, most faithful and dearest fellow-minister Philip Melanchthon, even as to the Tenth Article on the Sacred Supper — see Annot. I. §.6.
pass_a.300: The Number, reduced almost to Unity: not concerning the real Presence and Manducation of Christ’s body and blood in the supper — supernatural and spiritual — conceded on both sides, but concerning Presence occurring in, with, and under the bread, and oral manducation of both unworthy and worthy Communicants.
pass_a.301: The Mode of treating: peaceful and such as befits; a Theological Controversy held by both contending parties to be less fundamental, so that room may remain for fraternal and Christian charity.
pass_a.302: This Class of Theological controversies, to whatever number it is finally extended, between Lutherans and Reformed, as to the matter, is no other than such as still flourishes among Lutherans themselves (e.g. on Omnipresence and Multipresence of Christ’s Body) or among the Reformed (e.g. on Universal and Particular Grace) — derogating nothing whatever from Ecclesiastical Union.
pass_a.303: Whence there is no doubt that, as Fraternity once initiated with these Lutherans was recognized by the Reformed — both in Germany among the Marburgers and Rintelners at Cassel, and in Poland at Sendomir among those of the Augsburg, Bohemian, and Helvetic Confession — so the Reformed even today, as always elsewhere, openly profess that Christian Fraternity stands between them and such Lutherans; and likewise that these Lutherans have joined their hearts and minds with the Reformed in fraternal love, though more secretly, held back from external profession of Fraternity by fear of Schism, lest the remaining Lutherans be split from them.
pass_a.304: For that the Reformed differ from them by no fundamental error at all, they have long held — no less than the Reformed have long acknowledged and celebrated these Lutherans as altogether immune from every fundamental error.

298: ANNOTATION VI. On the classes of controversies that stand between Evangelicals (pp. 353–356).
§. I. Our author quickly splits them into two major classes, marked off by a nearly threefold difference: authors, number, and the mode of handling the disputes.
299: The prior class, on his account, has as disputants Luther’s genuine disciples.
They admit Melanchthon’s milder, declared and explained Augsburg Confession — even Article X on the Sacred Supper — if not from the start, then afterward (see Annot. I. §.6).
300: The disputed number shrinks almost to one point.
Both sides already concede a real supernatural and spiritual presence and manducation of Christ’s body and blood in the supper.
What remains is presence in, with, and under the bread, plus oral eating by unworthy and worthy communicants alike.
301: The mode is peaceful — the kind that fits a theological fight.
Both parties treat the controversy as less than fundamental, so fraternal Christian charity still has room.
302: As to the matter, this class between Lutherans and Reformed is no different from disputes that still run inside each camp — Lutheran fights over the body’s omnipresence and multipresence, or Reformed fights over universal and particular grace.
While it lasts, it takes nothing away from church union.
303: So there is no doubt: the Reformed once recognized fraternity with these Lutherans — in Germany at Cassel among Marburgers and Rintelners, and in Poland at Sendomir among Augsburg, Bohemian, and Helvetic confessionists.
They still openly profess that Christian fraternity with such Lutherans.
These Lutherans have joined heart and mind to the Reformed in brotherly love, even if more secretly — held back from an external profession by fear of schism with the rest of their own.
304: They have long held that the Reformed differ from them by no fundamental error at all.
The Reformed, for their part, have long acknowledged and celebrated these Lutherans as free of every fundamental error.
Stop before §. II (Posterior Class — Brenz, Andreae, Hunnius, Flacius / Formula of Concord).
